title: The Danger of False Dichotomies (And They Are All Technically False)
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay challenges leaders' reflexive use of dichotomies, good/evil, strong/weak, short-term/long-term, as mental shortcuts for making sense of complex people and situations. It argues that forcing reality into two opposing camps erases the gray area where accurate understanding and better decisions actually live. The author distinguishes between a simple description (a colleague is smart) and a false dichotomy (all colleagues are smart or dumb), showing how the latter distorts judgment. It suggests that the more expert a leader becomes in a subject, the less useful dichotomous thinking becomes, and urges readers to audit which either/or frames they've carried forward without examining them. The piece ends by tying nuanced thinking to genuinely simple, well-grounded conclusions rather than superficial simplicity.
points: Dichotomies save mental effort but usually erase the nuance and gray area that actually explain people and situations accurately.
There's a critical difference between describing one colleague as smart and dichotomizing all colleagues into smart-or-dumb camps.
The more sophisticated a leader's knowledge of a subject, the less useful dichotomous thinking becomes for that domain.
Leaders should audit inherited either/or frames, many were adopted young or during inexperience and never re-examined.
quotes: By creating a distinct demarcation between two competing endpoints, leaders are charged with deciding which side of the dichotomy best explains a person, situation, or event.
Unfortunately, dichotomies as fixed points are usually false. Or stated more accurately, they fail to recognize the gray between the black and white.
There is a difference between describing a colleague as smart (description) versus categorizing all colleagues as smart or dumb (dichotomy).
In fact, the more sophisticated a leader’s knowledge about a given subject matter, the less useful dichotomies are.
Simplicity emerges best from deep understanding, not from more simplicity.
